titre: Galois's Letter to Chevalier: What It Says About the Eve of the Duel
accroche: On the eve of the duel, Galois sums up his work in a letter. His first memoir had been written for more than sixteen months.
contenu_vulgarise:
The legend can be told in one sentence: in the night of May 29 to 30, 1832, Évariste Galois, twenty years old, supposedly dashed down the whole theory of groups on paper before going off to fight a duel. In 1982, Scientific American, from the pen of Tony Rothman, presents this story as a legend and adds that Galois's ideas took longer to mature. The MacTutor entry judges that it seems exaggerated.

## The Letter Itself

The document exists and can be read online. It is a letter dated “Paris, May 29, 1832,” addressed to his friend Auguste Chevalier. It opens with an inventory: “I have done several new things in analysis.” Galois announces three memoirs, then sums up the essentials: in which cases an equation is solvable by radicals (that is, by roots, like the quadratic formula), the way the group of its permutations can be decomposed, modular equations for the prime numbers 5, 7, and 11, integrals of algebraic functions.

The chronology is given by the letter itself. Of the first memoir, he writes: “The first is written, and despite what Poisson said of it, I stand by it with the corrections I have made.” A version of this memoir had been submitted to the Académie des sciences on January 17, 1831, sixteen months earlier, at Poisson's invitation, and Poisson had then judged it neither clear enough nor developed enough for its rigor to be assessed. A little further on: “everything I have written here has been in my head for nearly a year now.” The letter is not an improvised theory, it is a summary.

## Where Time Runs Short

The “I do not have the time” of the letter does not concern the whole. It closes a paragraph on a single field, which Galois describes as the search, a priori, for the exchanges of quantities that leave a relation between transcendental functions true: “But I do not have the time and my ideas are not yet well developed in this field, which is immense.” The rest is presented as established: “it is too much in my interest not to be mistaken for anyone to suspect me of having stated theorems of which I would not have the complete proof.” A marginal note in a manuscript, which MacTutor dates to the night before the duel, likewise says that a proof remains to be completed, for lack of time.

## The Readers He Chooses for Himself

Galois charges Chevalier with having the letter printed in the *Revue encyclopédique* (*Encyclopedic Review*) and with publicly asking Jacobi or Gauss to give their opinion not on the truth of the theorems, but on their importance. He hopes there will be readers to “decipher all this mess.”

The duel takes place on May 30, and Galois dies at the Cochin hospital the next day. His brother and Chevalier copy out his papers and send them to Gauss, to Jacobi, and to others, but no response is known. Joseph Liouville announces to the Académie, in September 1843, that he has found in these papers a solution judged as exact as it is profound, and publishes the manuscripts in his journal in 1846, fourteen years after the night of the duel.

carte.punch: Galois did not invent his theory on the eve of the duel: his letter sums up work already written.
carte.idee: In his letter to Chevalier of May 29, 1832, Galois writes that his first memoir is written and that his ideas have been in his head for nearly a year. The “I do not have the time” concerns only one unfinished field. A version of the memoir had been submitted to the Académie sixteen months earlier.

quiz.question: What do Galois's letter to Chevalier and its context show about the legend of the night of the duel?
choix: That he sets out his theory there for the first time, written in one go that night
That he gives up his results on equations there, judged false by Poisson
That it sums up work already written, including a memoir submitted to the Académie sixteen months earlier
That he asks the Académie to reopen the examination of his memoir
quiz.explication: The letter says that the first memoir is written, that he stands by it despite Poisson, and that his results have been in his head for nearly a year; a version had been submitted to the Académie on January 17, 1831. He gives up nothing, and it is Jacobi and Gauss, not the Académie, whom he wants to have asked for an opinion. The “no time” concerns only transcendental analysis.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How had Poisson judged Galois's first memoir, submitted to the Académie in January 1831?
choix: That it was neither clear enough nor developed enough for its rigor to be assessed
That it lacked novelty compared with work already published
That he had not had time to read it
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Poisson had judged Galois's first memoir neither clear enough nor developed enough for its rigor to be assessed, which the letter recalls by saying he stands by it despite that opinion. He did not call it wrong, it did not lack novelty, and Poisson had indeed read it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happened to Galois's papers after his death?
choix: Published without delay by the Académie des sciences
Lost before his brother could copy them out
Judged incomprehensible by Liouville, who sets them aside
Sent to Gauss and Jacobi, with no known response
quiz_supplementaire.explication: After Galois's death, his brother and Chevalier copy out his papers and send them to Gauss and Jacobi, with no known response, and Liouville publishes them only in 1846, fourteen years later, far from a rejection or a loss before copying.
